questions.problem: Given that $\frac{3}{4}+\sqrt{3}\text{i}=a+b\text{i}$, calculate the value of $a$ and the value of $b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we equate the real parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we equate the imaginary parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & =b\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=\frac{3}{4}$ and $b=\sqrt{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Product and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2-3\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3p+2q\text{i}}{2-3\text{i}} & =1+2\text{i} \\ 3p+2q\text{i} & =(1+2\text{i})(2-3\text{i}) \\ 3p+2q\text{i} & =2-3\text{i}+4\text{i}-6{\text{i}}^{2} \\ 3p+2q\text{i} & =2+\text{i}-6(-1) \\ 3p+2q\text{i} & =8+\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =8 \\ p & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =1 \\ q & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{8}{3}$ and $q=\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Quotient and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $3+2\text{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}5-\text{i} & =(p+\text{i}q)(3+2\text{i}) \\ \frac{5-\text{i}}{3+2\text{i}} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(5-\text{i})(3-2\text{i})}{(3+2\text{i})(3-2\text{i})} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{15-3\text{i}-10\text{i}+2{\text{i}}^{2}}{{3}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{13-13\text{i}}{9+4} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{13-13\text{i}}{13} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 1-\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $1=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $-1=q.$

Therefore, $p=1$ and $q=-1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Quotient and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $3+\text{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =(p+q\text{i})(3+\text{i}) \\ \frac{5}{3+\text{i}} & =p+q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(5)(3-\text{i})}{(3+\text{i})(3-\text{i})} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{15-5\text{i}}{{3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{15-5\text{i}}{9+1} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{15-5\text{i}}{10} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i} & =p+q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $\frac{3}{2}=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $-\frac{1}{2}=q.$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{2}$ and $q=-\frac{1}{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2-3\text{i} & =\frac{p-2q\text{i}}{1+2\text{i}} \\ (2-3\text{i})(1+2\text{i}) & =p-2q\text{i} \\ 2+4\text{i}-3\text{i}-6{\text{i}}^{2} & =p-2q\text{i} \\ 2+\text{i}-6(-1) & =p-2q\text{i} \\ 8+\text{i} & =p-2q\text{i}\end{aligned}
